channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: Norm and I Adore Satire and Yoga
item.description: Barry Humphries returns to Melbourne from London, more polished and confident, with a new show at the Comedy Theatre, an updated Mrs Norm Everage who now does yoga and hangs her own pasta on the clothesline, and stories of waiting outside the Savoy in drag to ambush the Prime Minister.

item.title: You Can't Get Much Lusher
item.description: The Fabulous Lido, a lavish theatre-restaurant in Melbourne's old Savoy building, is about to open, with millionaire ex-dancer David Hamilton McIlwraith pouring half a million pounds into gold mosaic tiles, chandeliers imported from Egypt and long-legged hand-picked showgirls.

item.title: Keeping up with Carnaby Street
item.description: British fashion designers Roger Nelson and Jean Muir arrive in Melbourne to present the mod Regency look for men, double-breasted with six buttons and floral shirts, and confirm that Melbourne's Lord Henry's Gear store in Russell Street is right up with the latest in Carnaby Street.

item.title: Dawn of a New Golden Age
item.description: A behind-the-scenes account of the lavish promotional campaign Hoyts mounted for the Melbourne premiere of Goldfinger, from painted-gold television models and purloined Bond-girl display panels to kits containing white roses and toy revolvers.

item.title: A Marvellous Auction Sale
item.description: A charity auction for Melbourne's Cultural Centre raises funds through improbable lots — LBJ's hat, Patrick White's autographed plays, Dita Cobb's false eyelashes — while the centre itself remains mired in a naming dispute between 'National Gallery and Art Centre of Victoria' and the simpler 'Artorium'.

item.title: What Sort of School?
item.description: A two-part examination of the class anxieties and practical calculations behind Melbourne parents' choices between state and private schools, with Batman weighing snobbery, church, facilities and self-confidence, and philosopher Max Charlesworth arguing from John Stuart Mill for the Catholic right to choose.

item.title: Bolte Plays Ring-a-rosy
item.description: Melbourne's almost total absence of freeways, while Sydney and American cities forge ahead, traced to the Victorian Country Party's stranglehold on the Legislative Council and its repeated blocking of Henry Bolte's road-funding proposals.

item.title: No Openings for Henry Bolte
item.description: The insurance building boom transforms Melbourne's William Street, with Sir Robert Menzies cornering the market on grand openings while the old St James building makes way for a new AMP tower designed by American architects Skidmore, Owings and Merrill.

item.title: The Big Strike and Late Closing
item.description: A sardonic dispatch from strike-bound Melbourne in February 1966, where a Victorian public servants' walkout brought empty city bars, warm beer and candlelight, while the pubs that survived thrived under the newly extended 10 o'clock trading hours, and Chloe continued to bare all at Young and Jackson's for another 30 hours a week.

item.title: Who's Been Working on the Railroad?
item.description: Melbourne's underground railway dream traces a 40-year history of reports, promises, shelved starts and lottery schemes, from the 1929 Metropolitan Town Planning Commission report through the Utah Construction Company's flat offer to build in three years, to the Wilbur Smith and Associates study of 1966 that recommends the same underground the city has been talking about since 1925.

item.title: The Battle of the Sly Bakers: 90,000 Illegal Loaves
item.description: Melbourne's long-running underground war over illegal weekend bread baking, where 90,000 families buy fresh loaves from clandestine Sunday bakeries while union officials and the Trades Hall Council condemn the practice as sweated labour in unsanitary conditions.

item.title: The Great Football Fade-out
item.description: A statistical and cultural argument that Melbourne's claim to be the world's greatest football city is overstated, with crowd figures failing to keep pace with population growth and a large section of the community only going through the motions of football devotion.

item.title: It Never Rains in the Mallee
item.description: The opening of Australia's first full-scale Folk Museum at Swan Hill, built around the restored paddlesteamer Gem and a growing collection of Mallee farming machinery, with Sir Henry Bolte presiding over a sodden ceremony that proved the museum's name something of a misnomer.

item.title: Courage, Not to Stumble, Brother
item.description: The history of Victoria's beer monopoly under Carlton and United Breweries, and the arrival of the Courage Brewery of England with plans for a $11 million Melbourne plant, raising the question of whether hotelkeepers will dare switch allegiances.

item.title: Getting into Troubled Waters
item.description: The long history of the Victoria-South Australia border dispute, from the 1839 survey through successive High Court and Privy Council cases to the 1966 standoff over offshore oil rights, with Sir Henry Bolte threatening a blockade of Corio whisky and Melbourne Cup horses.

item.title: In a State over Hanging
item.description: Victoria's troubled history with capital punishment, from the 1951 triple execution of Jean Lee, Norman Andrews and Robert Clayton to the 1962 Robert Peter Tait case, and the imminent hanging of Ronald Ryan for the murder of prison warder George Hodson, with Premier Sir Henry Bolte refusing all deputations or reprieve.

item.title: Art on a pastoral binge: wine, food, and fantasy
item.description: A tour of the gallery movement sweeping Victoria's provincial towns, from the Hamilton Shaw Collection to Ballarat's hotbed of Lindsays and the new Mildura Arts Centre, where the third Mildura Prize for Sculpture drew a washing-machine agitator with a Ford Thunderbird tail-light and a taxi driver who reckoned the winner was two giraffes mating.

item.title: Here's, perhaps, another place for a future village
item.description: The case for Westernport Bay as Melbourne's future industrial port, measuring the bay's natural advantages against Port Phillip's treacherous entrance and Corsair Rock, as BP's new Crib Point refinery, a coming Esso oil refinery, and John Lysaght's steel works promise to transform the area.

item.title: They're high, wide, handsome and available
item.description: Melbourne's office building boom has produced towers with prestige address plaques and embarrassingly empty floors, as the city discovers it cannot breed white-collar workers fast enough to fill the marble palaces rising across the CBD.

item.title: Talking Turkey and a little Gaelic about football
item.description: The MCG's spectacular new western stand, with its cantilever overhangs, beer reticulation system and a scoreboard 115 feet above street level, is completed just in time for the finals, while Ron Barassi prepares to take a team to Dublin despite a Gaelic Athletic Association rule book that threatens suspension for anyone who plays or even attends cricket.

item.title: No more bed and board for our Cliveden set
item.description: A history of Cliveden Mansions in East Melbourne, the grand apartment hotel built in 1887 by Sir William Clarke, tracing its rise as a resort of the colonial gentry and its long decline into an era of plastic flowers and electric rooftop signs.

item.title: Among the Pasties
item.description: A tour of Sydney's King's Cross strip clubs, from the Pink Pussy Cat to the Crazy Horse, appraising the performers, the audiences and the bizarre economics of a world where a good stripper earns seventy pounds a week and can appear at three clubs a night.

item.title: All the Fun of the Ferry
item.description: A report on Melbourne's Moomba festival, tracing how it grew from the old Eight-hour Day trade union procession into a city-wide holiday spectacle, with Sydney's Manly ferry North Head the unexpected hit of the week on the Yarra.

item.title: Just an Anonymous Airport
item.description: The Federal Government's failure to fund terminal buildings at Melbourne's new Tullamarine airport reignites the Melbourne-Sydney rivalry, with Melbourne's Tullamarine boosters warning the city risks disappearing from international air maps entirely.

item.title: Dogs Chasing Each Other's Tails
item.description: The 14th Australian Architectural Convention debates the chaotic state of Melbourne's planning, with Harry Seidler lamenting the two-to-one height formula and architects mourning the imminent demolition of Walter Burley Griffin's Capitol Theatre for a shopping arcade.

item.title: Batman Crosses the Murray
item.description: A visit to Sydney forces a grudging admission that the city is gaining an edge on Melbourne, with superior old and new buildings, easier taxi access, cheaper public transport and a Sydney Opera House that, from a distance at least, looks glorious.

item.title: Wanted, a Civic Symbol
item.description: The case for Melbourne's proposed Lower Yarra bridge as the city's long-missing civic symbol, with a detailed comparison of its planned dimensions against the Sydney Harbour Bridge and a sidelight on the Rebecca Riots as a precedent for toll-gate fury.

item.title: Which City is in Front...?
item.description: A survey of the Melbourne versus Sydney rivalry, examining competing newspaper claims about population growth, migration, new industries, building completions and personal income, prompted by the CIA-level precision with which LBJ's visit was split equally between the two cities.

item.title: The other Edinburgh (Part two of two parts)
item.description: The second part of the centenary retelling of Prince Alfred's 1867 Australian tour: the shooting of the Duke at Clontarf by Henry O'Farrell, the wave of anti-Irish feeling it unleashed across the colonies, O'Farrell's trial and execution, and HMS Galatea's quiet departure.

item.title: As conspicuous as a negro at a KKK picnic
item.description: Keith Dunstan reports on Little Stevie Wonder's Australian tour, tracing the pandemonium of 7000 fans at a Sydney concert where police, security men and ambulance officers struggled to contain girls aged 14 to 17 fainting, weeping and tearing at their own hair, and contrasting the hysteria with the singer's composed, almost supernatural stage presence.
